name: Odia
where: Odisha (official language), plus neighbouring parts of Jharkhand, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh and Andhra Pradesh
tagline: A classical language with a beautifully rounded script, gentle sounds and no grammatical gender — the key to Odisha's temples, coast and kitchens.
intro:
**Odia** (ଓଡ଼ିଆ, formerly spelled *Oriya*) is the language of Odisha on India's east coast. It is an Indo-Aryan language, a close cousin of Bengali and Assamese and more distantly of Hindi, and in 2014 it was recognised as one of India's *classical languages* thanks to a written tradition stretching back over a thousand years.

Odia has its own script, instantly recognisable by its round, umbrella-like tops. Like Devanagari it is an *abugida*: each consonant carries a built-in vowel, here pronounced **ô** (as in British *hot*), and other vowels are added as signs around the consonant. Unlike Hindi, Odia **keeps** that vowel at the end of words: ଘର is *ghôrô*, not *ghar*.

The grammar is friendly to English speakers in one big way: there is **no grammatical gender** — verbs and adjectives never change for male or female, and there is no ergative construction in the past tense. Instead, verbs change for **person** and **politeness**: Odia has three levels of *you* — respectful **ଆପଣ** (*apôṇô*), familiar **ତୁମେ** (*tume*) and intimate **ତୁ** (*tu*). Nouns take case endings (-କୁ, -ରେ, -ରୁ, -ର) and counting words (classifiers) such as **ଟି**, **ଟା** and **ଜଣ**.

This course teaches the standard spoken Odia of Cuttack and Bhubaneswar — the variety heard on Odia TV and radio and understood across the state — and points out colloquial forms you will hear on the street. You will learn the script, the sounds, numbers and twenty units of everyday language, from greetings to telling stories.
romanizationNote: The romanization shows how words are **said**. The inherent vowel ଅ is written **ô** (the vowel of British *hot* or American *thought*, lips slightly rounded) and — unlike Hindi — it is pronounced at the end of words too: ଘର *ghôrô*, ନାମ *namô*, ଭାତ *bhatô*; only a word written with the hasanta (୍) or an English loanword ends in a bare consonant (ଠିକ୍ *ṭhik*, ବସ୍ *bôs*). ଆ is plain **a** (as in *father*); Odia has no long/short vowel contrast, so ଇ/ଈ are both **i** and ଉ/ଊ both **u**, and no macrons are used. ଏ is **e** (as in *café*), ଓ is **o** (as in *go*, without the glide), ଐ/ଔ are **ôi/ôu**. **ṭ ṭh ḍ ḍh ṇ** are retroflex (tongue curled back); plain **t th d dh n** are dental (tongue touching the teeth) — never English t/d. **ṛ ṛh** are the flaps ଡ଼ ଢ଼, and **ḷ** is the retroflex ଳ, a separate sound from ଲ *l*. All three sibilants ଶ ଷ ସ are pronounced **s** in standard Odia, so we write *s* (ଶୀତ *sitô*). Both ଜ and ଯ sound like English **j**; ୟ is **y**. **ch** is unaspirated, **chh** aspirated; an *h* after any consonant means a puff of breath (*kh, gh, th, dh, ph, bh*), so *ph* is not f and *th* is never as in *the*. **ṃ** after a vowel means the vowel is nasalised (ଚନ୍ଦ୍ରବିନ୍ଦୁ ଁ: ମୁଁ *muṃ*, ହଁ *hôṃ*); the anusvara ଂ is a real **ṅ** (as in *sing*): ସିଂହ *siṅhô*. Consonants written double are held longer (*kk, tt*); the ଯ-ଫଳା (୍ୟ) doubles the consonant before it (ବିଦ୍ୟା *biddya*). କ୍ଷ is *khy* and ଜ୍ଞ is *gy*, and the vowel ଋ / ୃ is *ru* (କୃଷକ *krusôkô*). Proper nouns are capitalised; Odia language names are capitalised too (*Oṛia*, *Iṅraji*).

script.overview:
The Odia script (ଓଡ଼ିଆ ଲିପି) descends, like Devanagari and Bengali, from the ancient Brahmi script, but it looks very different: almost every letter is crowned by a round arch called the **ଛତା** (*chhôta*, "umbrella"). The usual explanation is that Odia was written for centuries with an iron stylus on dried palm leaves, where long straight horizontal lines (like the Devanagari headline) would split the leaf — so scribes used curves instead. There is no headline joining letters together; each syllable stands on its own.

Odia is an **abugida**. A bare consonant letter already includes the vowel **ô**: କ is *kô*, ମ is *mô*. To give a consonant a different vowel you attach a **vowel sign** (ଫଳା/ମାତ୍ରା): କା *ka*, କି *ki*, କୁ *ku*, କେ *ke*, କୋ *ko*. Signs can sit to the right (ା ୀ), below (ୁ ୂ ୃ), to the left (େ) or around the consonant (ୋ ୌ). The full vowel letters (ଅ ଆ ଇ …) are used only at the start of a word or after another vowel. Unlike Hindi, the inherent ô is normally **pronounced even at the end of a word** (କଥା *kôtha*, ଘର *ghôrô*).

To show a consonant with no vowel at all you use the **hasanta** (୍), but much more often two consonants join into a **conjunct** (ଯୁକ୍ତାକ୍ଷର). In Odia the second consonant is usually written smaller *underneath* the first (a so-called *ଫଳା* form): ନ୍ତ, ମ୍ବ, ସ୍ତ. Some second consonants take special shapes: ର-ଫଳା (୍ର) is a little hook below (ପ୍ର), ଯ-ଫଳା (୍ୟ) a small mark to the right (ବିଦ୍ୟା), ବ-ଫଳା (୍ୱ) a small curl below (ସ୍ୱ). A ର before another consonant becomes the **ରେଫ**, a small hook on top (କର୍ମ). A few conjuncts, such as କ୍ଷ and ଜ୍ଞ, look like brand-new letters.

The script is written left to right. The full stop is the vertical bar **।** (*daṇḍô*); commas and question marks are as in English. Odia also has its own digits (୦–୯), still used in newspapers, calendars and signboards alongside Western numerals.

groups.title: Vowels (ସ୍ୱରବର୍ଣ୍ଣ)
groups.note: Odia has 11 vowel letters in everyday use. Each has an independent form (used at the start of a word or after another vowel) and a sign form attached to consonants. Long and short i and u are spelled differently but sound the same. Old schoolbooks also list ୠ, ଌ, ୡ, which never occur in modern words.

pronunciation.title: ଅ (ô) versus ଆ (a)
pronunciation.body:
The single most important vowel contrast in Odia is between the inherent vowel **ଅ ô** and **ଆ a**. ô is a rounded back vowel — the *o* of British *hot* or the *aw* of *law*, said short. a is an open, unrounded *ah*. English speakers tend to say both as 'uh' (as in *cup*), which makes Odia words impossible to tell apart.

To get ô, make your lips slightly round, as if starting to say *o*, and drop your jaw. For a, keep the lips spread and the mouth wide open. Every consonant letter without a vowel sign carries ô, so this sound is everywhere.
tips: Never say 'uh' for ô — think 'aw' with rounded lips.
a (ଆ) is like the a in 'father', short and open.
Practise in front of a mirror: lips round for ô, spread for a.

pronunciation.title: Keep the final ô (no schwa deletion)
pronunciation.body:
If you know Hindi, beware: Hindi drops the inherent vowel at the end of words (घर *ghar*, नाम *nām*), but **Odia pronounces it**: ଘର *ghôrô*, ନାମ *namô*. It is short and light, but it is there, and leaving it off makes you sound like a Hindi or Bengali speaker.

The final ô often makes a grammatical difference. Many familiar (ତୁମେ) commands end in -ô, while related nouns end in -a: ଦେଖ *dekhô* 'look!' versus ଦେଖା *dekha* 'a meeting'. The vowel is only absent when a word is written with the hasanta (୍), mostly in loanwords and a few short words (ଠିକ୍ *ṭhik*, ବସ୍ *bôs*).
tips: Finish every word written without a final vowel sign with a short 'aw'.
Don't stress the final ô — Odia stress is light and falls near the start of the word.
A written hasanta (୍) means: no vowel.

pronunciation.title: Vowel sequences: ପୁଅ, ଝିଅ, ଗାଈ
pronunciation.body:
Odia loves strings of vowels with no consonant between them. The written vowel letter ଅ after another vowel is a separate short ô syllable: ପୁଅ *pu-ô* 'son', ଝିଅ *jhi-ô* 'daughter', ଛଅ *chhô* 'six' (here the two ô's merge). Likewise ଗାଈ is *ga-i* 'cow', ବୋଉ *bo-u* 'mum', ଖାଇବା *kha-i-ba* 'to eat'.

Pronounce each vowel clearly and glide smoothly from one to the next — don't insert a *y* or *w*, and don't collapse them into an English diphthong.
tips: Count the vowels: ପୁଅ has two syllables, ଖାଇବା has three.
Keep each vowel pure; no 'y' or 'w' between them.
ଏଇ and ସେଇ (this/that) are e-i, se-i.

pairs.note: ପୁଅ ends in rounded ô, ପୁଆ in open a.
Same sound — only the spelling of i differs.

pronunciation.title: Long and short vowels sound the same
pronunciation.body:
Odia spelling keeps the Sanskrit distinction between short ଇ/ି and long ଈ/ୀ, and short ଉ/ୁ and long ଊ/ୂ. But in modern speech they are **pronounced identically**: medium-length *i* and *u*. That is good news for speaking — you only have to remember the difference for writing.

Some word pairs are spelled differently but sound exactly the same; context tells you which is meant. This course writes both simply as *i* and *u*.
tips: Say ଇ and ଈ the same; same for ଉ and ଊ.
When writing, learn the spelling word by word.
Final -ି and -ୀ are both just 'i'.

pronunciation.title: Aspiration: k vs kh, d vs dh
pronunciation.body:
Odia distinguishes plain consonants from **aspirated** ones, which are followed by a clear puff of breath: କ *k* / ଖ *kh*, ଗ *g* / ଘ *gh*, ଚ *ch* / ଛ *chh*, ଜ *j* / ଝ *jh*, ଟ / ଠ, ଡ / ଢ, ତ / ଥ, ଦ / ଧ, ପ / ଫ, ବ / ଭ.

English speakers have two problems. First, English p, t, k at the start of a word already have a small puff, so Odia plain ପ ତ କ (no puff) sound to you like b d g — practise them like the p in *spin*. Second, the voiced aspirates ଘ ଝ ଢ ଧ ଭ don't exist in English: say the voiced sound and let a breathy h follow, as in *doghouse*, *clubhouse*.
tips: Hold a tissue in front of your mouth: it should move for ଖ ଫ ଥ, not for କ ପ ତ.
ph is a p with breath, never an f; th/dh never like English 'th'.
For bh, gh, dh: start the voice, then breathe out — 'club-house'.

pronunciation.title: Retroflex vs dental consonants
pronunciation.body:
Odia has two sets of t/d sounds where English has one. The **dental** ତ ଥ ଦ ଧ ନ are made with the tongue tip pressed against the back of the upper teeth — softer and more forward than English t/d. The **retroflex** ଟ ଠ ଡ ଢ ଣ are made with the tongue tip curled back to touch the roof of the mouth behind the gum ridge — they sound hollow and 'heavy'.

English t and d are made in between, on the gum ridge, so Odia speakers hear them as retroflex. Practise exaggerating both: tongue between/against the teeth for ତ, tongue curled right back for ଟ.
tips: For ତ ଦ ନ, the tongue should touch your teeth.
For ଟ ଡ ଣ, curl the tip backwards and strike the roof of the mouth.
English loanwords with t/d (ଟେବୁଲ, ଡାକ୍ତର) use the retroflex set.

pairs.note: Both the t and the n differ.
Near pair: compare the first consonants.

pronunciation.title: The flaps ଡ଼ and ଢ଼
pronunciation.body:
ଡ଼ (*ṛ*) and ଢ଼ (*ṛh*) are made by curling the tongue tip back and then **flicking** it forward so it brushes the roof of the mouth once on its way down. The result sounds somewhere between a d and an r. ଢ଼ is the same with a breath.

They never start a word; they appear between vowels and at the end of words: ବଡ଼ *bôṛô* 'big', ଘୋଡ଼ା *ghoṛa* 'horse', ପଢ଼ *pôṛhô* 'read!'. Don't replace them with English d (too hard) or with the tapped ର (too forward).
tips: Curl the tongue back, then let it fall forward — one quick flick.
ର is tapped at the gum ridge; ଡ଼ is flicked from far back.
The name of the language itself has one: ଓଡ଼ିଆ Oṛia.

pronunciation.title: ଳ versus ଲ
pronunciation.body:
Odia has two l-sounds. ଲ (*l*) is an ordinary clear l. ଳ (*ḷ*) is **retroflex**: curl the tongue tip back, as for ଡ, and then say l. It is very common in native Odia words (ଜଳ, ଫଳ, କଳା, ସକାଳ) and makes real differences in meaning.

In fast colloquial speech some people blur the two, but standard Odia keeps them apart — and the pairs below show why.
tips: ଳ = l with the tongue curled back.
Say ଡ, then keep the tongue there and let air flow round the sides: ଳ.
Don't confuse ଳ (ḷ) with the flap ଡ଼ (ṛ): ଳ is a continuous l.

pronunciation.title: Nasal consonants: ଣ, ନ, ଙ, ଞ, ମ and ଂ
pronunciation.body:
Odia has a full set of nasal consonants matching each place of articulation. The two you must actively practise are **ଣ** (retroflex n — tongue curled back, very common: ପାଣି, ଶୁଣ, ଲୁଣ) and **ନ** (dental n — tongue on the teeth).

ଙ (*ṅ*) and ଞ (*ñ*) appear almost only inside conjuncts, where the nasal simply takes the position of the next consonant: ଙ୍କ *ṅk*, ଙ୍ଗ *ṅg*, ଞ୍ଚ *ñch*. The anusvara ଂ is a full *ng* sound (ସିଂହ *siṅhô*), unlike the chandrabindu ଁ, which only nasalises a vowel.
tips: ଣ in ପାଣି: curl the tongue back before the n.
ଙ୍କ/ଙ୍ଗ are 'nk'/'ng' as in 'bank', 'finger'.
ଂ is a consonant 'ng'; ଁ is a nasal vowel.

pairs.note: Near pair: retroflex ṇ versus dental n.

pronunciation.title: Nasal vowels (ଁ)
pronunciation.body:
The chandrabindu ଁ makes the vowel before it **nasal**: air flows through the nose and mouth together, as in French *non* or *bien*. There is no n or m consonant at the end — just a nasal colour on the vowel. Some of the most common words have it: ମୁଁ *muṃ* 'I', ହଁ *hôṃ* 'yes', ନାହିଁ *nahiṃ* 'no / is not', ପାଇଁ *paiṃ* 'for'.

It also matters grammatically: honorific and plural case forms add a nasal (ତାକୁ *taku* 'to him' vs ତାଙ୍କୁ *taṅku* 'to him (respectful)').
tips: Hum slightly through your nose while saying the vowel.
Don't add a full n at the end of ମୁଁ — it's 'muṃ', not 'moon'.
Pinch your nose: a nasal vowel will sound blocked.

pronunciation.title: One s for three letters; ଯ is j, ୟ is y
pronunciation.body:
Odia spelling inherited three s-letters from Sanskrit — ଶ, ଷ and ସ — but standard Odia pronounces **all three as s** (as in *sun*). Speakers of Hindi or Bengali often say *sh*; in Odia that sounds bookish or foreign. A *sh* is heard only in some English loanwords and careful Sanskrit recitation.

Similarly there are two y-letters: **ଯ** (*borgiya jô*) is pronounced **j**, exactly like ଜ, while **ୟ** (*ontôsthô yô*, with a dot/slash below) is a real *y*. So ଯାତ୍ରା is *jatra*, ଯଦି is *jôdi*, but ନିୟମ is *niyômô*. The letter ୱ is *w*, mostly in conjuncts (ସ୍ୱ *sw*).
tips: Read every ଶ ଷ ସ as s.
ଯ = j; ୟ = y.
ବ is always b: Sanskrit 'v' words are said with b (ବିଦେଶ *bidesô*).

pronunciation.title: Letters that don't sound like their spelling: ଋ, କ୍ଷ, ଜ୍ଞ
pronunciation.body:
A few Sanskrit letters have a typically Odia pronunciation. The vowel **ଋ / ୃ** is said **ru** (Hindi says *ri*): ଋତୁ *rutu* 'season', କୃଷକ *krusôkô* 'farmer'. The conjunct **କ୍ଷ** is said **khy** (Hindi *kṣ*): କ୍ଷୀର *khyirô* 'milk', ଶିକ୍ଷକ *sikhyôkô* 'teacher'. **ଜ୍ଞ** is said **gy**: ଜ୍ଞାନ *gyanô* 'knowledge', ଆଜ୍ଞା *agya* 'sir; yes sir'.

And the ଯ-ଫଳା (୍ୟ) doubles the consonant before it: ଧନ୍ୟବାଦ *dhônnyôbadô*, ବିଦ୍ୟା *biddya*, ସତ୍ୟ *sôttyô*.
tips: ୃ = ru, never ri.
କ୍ଷ = khy; ଜ୍ଞ = gy.
୍ୟ: hold the consonant before it longer.

pronunciation.title: Double consonants
pronunciation.body:
A doubled consonant is **held** for longer before releasing: ପକ୍କା *pôkka* has a clear pause on the k, like the 'k-c' in *book-case*. Single and double consonants can change the meaning, so don't rush through them.

Doubling is written with a conjunct (କ୍କ, ତ୍ତ, ଲ୍ଲ, ଚ୍ଛ …) and also happens automatically before the ଯ-ଫଳା (୍ୟ).
tips: Pause briefly on the doubled consonant.
Think 'book-case', 'hot-tea'.
Single consonants between vowels are short and light.

pronunciation.title: Rhythm and question intonation
pronunciation.body:
Odia has a light, even rhythm: syllables are of similar length and there is no heavy English-style stress. A gentle prominence falls on the **first syllable** of a word. Don't reduce unstressed vowels to 'uh' — every ô and a keeps its full quality.

A yes/no question can be made just by **raising the pitch** at the end of a statement: ସେ ଆସିବ। (falling) 'He will come.' vs ସେ ଆସିବ? (rising) 'Will he come?'. You can also add the particle **କି** (*ki*) at the end: ତୁମେ ଖାଇଛ କି? 'Have you eaten?'. Question-word questions (କ'ଣ, କେଉଁଠି…) usually fall at the end.
tips: Keep syllables even; don't swallow vowels.
Rise at the end for yes/no questions; fall for 'what/where' questions.
କି at the end turns a statement into a question.
